intro: A sewing machine looks complicated until you have named its parts. Then it is a small set of jobs: a spool feeds thread down one fixed path, a bobbin feeds a second thread from below, a hook loops one around the other, and a lever pulls them tight, hundreds of times a minute. Almost everything that goes wrong at a machine, from a jam to a nest of loops to a seam that puckers, traces back to one of those jobs done out of order. This unit teaches you to see the machine that way, so that a problem is a checklist and not a mystery.

You will start with the machine itself: every part named, the top thread path in the right order with the presser foot up, a bobbin wound evenly and dropped in the right way round, and the lockstitch watched forming one slow turn of the hand wheel at a time. You will learn what the stitch length and width dials actually move, how to read the underside of a seam to tell loose tension from tight, and which needle belongs in which fabric. You will also learn the rules that keep fingers away from the needle and the cleaning that keeps a machine sewing for decades.

Then you will sew. A straight seam on the 5/8-inch line, locked at both ends with backstitches. A square corner turned with the needle down. A raw edge finished so it cannot fray, and a seam pressed flat before anything crosses it. All of it comes together in a drawstring bag you plan, cut, sew, press and evaluate against your own numbers. By the end you will be able to sit at an unfamiliar machine, thread it from its manual, and fix it when it misbehaves.
bigQuestion: How does a sewer turn a machine, a spool and a bobbin into a seam that is straight, square, strong and flat every time?

timeline.t: Charles Weisenthal patents a double-pointed needle with an eye in the middle, meant for a machine
Thomas Saint of London patents a design for a machine to stitch leather
Barthélemy Thimonnier patents a chain-stitch machine in France and opens a workshop sewing uniforms
Walter Hunt of New York builds a lockstitch machine with an eye-pointed needle and a shuttle, but does not patent it
Elias Howe receives a U.S. patent for a lockstitch sewing machine
Isaac Singer patents a machine with a straight needle, a presser foot and a foot treadle
The main makers pool their patents in the Sewing Machine Combination, ending years of lawsuits
Singer offers an electric-motor sewing machine
The Singer Featherweight, a small portable electric machine, is introduced at the Chicago World's Fair
Zigzag home machines become common, making machine seam finishes and buttonholes routine
Electronic home machines add push-button stitch selection and speed control
Computerized machines offer hundreds of stitches, and a basic mechanical machine still makes the same lockstitch Howe patented

words.d: the arm that rises and falls with each stitch and pulls the top thread tight; the step beginners most often miss when threading
two plates that pinch the top thread; they open only when the presser foot is raised
the small flat spool under the throat plate that supplies the bottom thread
the machine stitch formed when the hook loops the top thread around the bobbin thread and the take-up lever locks it in the fabric
the teeth under the presser foot that move the fabric forward by one stitch length each stitch
a stitch where the two threads lock in the middle of the fabric so both sides look alike
a needle with a rounded tip for knits; it slides between the loops instead of cutting them
the fabric between the stitching and the raw edge; 5/8 inch on most patterns
three or four stitches sewn in reverse at the start and end of a seam to lock it
turning a corner with the needle down in the fabric and the presser foot lifted
a zigzag, pinked, serged or turned edge that stops a seam allowance from fraying
lifting and setting the iron on a seam, first closed and then open, rather than sliding it

test.q: Which part must be UP while you thread the top of the machine, and why?
choices: The presser foot, so the tension discs open
The needle, so the thread reaches it
The feed dogs, so the fabric is loose
The bobbin cover, so the thread drops in
test.why: Raising the presser foot opens the tension discs. Threading with the foot down leaves the thread lying on top of the discs with no tension.

test.q: Which part catches the loop of top thread and carries it around the bobbin?
test.why: The hook spins around the bobbin and catches the loop that forms behind the rising needle, wrapping it around the bobbin thread.

test.q: Loops of top thread show on the underside of the seam. What is the problem?
choices: The top thread is too tight
The top thread is too loose or not seated in the discs
test.why: Top thread pulled through to the bottom means too little top tension. Rethread with the foot up first, then adjust the dial if needed.

test.q: Which needle belongs in T-shirt knit?
test.why: A ballpoint's rounded tip slips between knit loops without cutting them, preventing runs and skipped stitches.

test.q: What is a good stitch length for an ordinary seam in medium cotton?
test.why: 2.5 mm, about 10 to 12 stitches per inch, is the everyday setting. 4 to 5 mm is for basting.

test.q: Which way do you turn the hand wheel?
test.why: The hand wheel always turns toward you. Turning it away can pull the thread out of the needle and jam the machine.

test.q: What is the first step before cleaning lint out from under the throat plate?
test.why: Hands go near the needle and moving parts, so the machine must be unplugged, not just off.

test.q: The standard seam allowance on most commercial patterns is:
test.why: 5/8 inch, about 1.5 cm, is the standard. The throat plate has a line for it.

test.q: What do the three or four reverse stitches at the start and end of a seam do?
choices: Lock the seam so it cannot pull open
test.why: Backstitching sews over the first and last stitches so the thread ends are anchored.

test.q: Before lifting the presser foot to pivot a corner, the needle should be:
test.why: The needle pins the fabric in place while you turn it, so the two seam lines meet at one point.

test.q: Which seam finish can a basic zigzag machine do to stop fraying?
choices: A medium zigzag over the raw edge
test.why: A zigzag over the edge wraps the loose fibers. A serger is a separate machine; pressing does not stop fraying.

test.q: What does "press, do not iron" mean for a fresh seam?
choices: Lift and set the iron instead of sliding it
Press only from the right side
test.why: Sliding stretches a freshly sewn seam. Pressing lifts the iron, sets it down in one spot, and moves on.

test.q: Two bag rectangles are cut 10 inches wide with 5/8-inch side seams. How wide is the finished bag?
test.why: Two seams take 1¼ inches in total. 10 minus 1¼ equals 8¾ inches.

test.q: A nest of loops has formed under the fabric and jammed the machine. After clearing it, what is the fix?
choices: Rethread the top with the presser foot up and hold the tails at the start
test.why: A nest underneath is a top-thread problem: the thread was not in the discs or the foot was up. Rethread and hold the tails.

test.q: A universal needle skips stitches on stretchy knit. Which change fixes it?
test.why: Knits need a ballpoint so the loop forms cleanly and the hook can catch it.

write.prompt: Write the complete plan for making a drawstring bag on a sewing machine, from threading the machine through the final press: every step in order, the tool or setting for each step (needle size, stitch length, seam allowance, casing folds), and the safety rule that applies. For each step, explain in one sentence why it comes where it does.
tips: Start at the machine: threading order with the foot up, bobbin wound and inserted, a test on a scrap before the project.
Give the numbers: cut size, 5/8-inch seams, the 1¾-inch cord opening, the ½-inch and 1¼-inch casing folds, cord length.
Name the moves at the start, the corner and the end of each seam: backstitch, pivot with the needle down, backstitch.
Say when each seam gets pressed and finished, and why it happens before the next seam crosses it.
End with how you will check the bag against your plan: measurements, seam widths, raw edges, and the drawstring test.
